title: Regression and the Normal Distribution — Slide Deck

slides.title: Regression and the Normal Distribution
slides.subtitle: Chapter 1 excerpt — Frees, Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications
bullets: Introduces regression's role in actuarial science
Covers the normal curve, transforms, sampling assumptions
Connects theory to pricing, reserving, and solvency testing
slides.speaker_notes: Open by framing regression as the central statistical tool of the book, then preview the chapter's arc from the normal curve to actuarial applications.
source_ids: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

slides.title: 1.1 What Is Regression Analysis?
slides.subtitle: Explaining a variable of interest
bullets: Statistics = collection, summarization, analysis of data
Regression: distinguishing feature is controlling for explanatory variables
Illustrated by Galton's 1885 parent-child height data (n=928)
24,000+ articles used regression over 1978-2007
slides.speaker_notes: Emphasize that regression's core value is isolating the relationship between a response and explanatory variables, using Galton's foundational dataset as the historical anchor.
source_ids: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

slides.title: 1.2 Fitting Data to a Normal Distribution
slides.subtitle: Two parameters summarize a distribution
bullets: Normal curve: f(y) = 1/(sigma*sqrt(2*pi)) * exp(-(y-mu)^2/2sigma^2)
mu = location, sigma^2 = scale
Example: MA bodily injury claims, n=272, mean 0.481 (log-thousands)
Box plots and qq plots diagnose fit
slides.speaker_notes: Walk through the normal density formula, then show how the MA claims example applies mean/median/std dev/percentiles in practice.
source_ids: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

slides.title: 1.3 Power Transforms
slides.subtitle: Symmetrizing skewed data with Box-Cox
bullets: Box-Cox family: y^(lambda) = (y^lambda-1)/lambda, or ln(y) when lambda=0
Common lambda values: 1, 1/2, 0, -1
Insurance claims are typically right-skewed
Log transform (lambda=0) often symmetrizes best
slides.speaker_notes: Explain why analysts reach for logs specifically, and show the chi-square(2) simulation as a controlled illustration of the four transform choices.
source_ids: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

slides.title: 1.4 Sampling and the Role of Normality
slides.subtitle: Four Basic Sampling Assumptions
bullets: E(y_i) = mu
Var(y_i) = sigma^2
{y_i} independent
{y_i} normally distributed
Normality (#4) often relaxed via CLT
slides.speaker_notes: Clarify that normality is the most dispensable of the four assumptions thanks to central limit theorems, unlike independence and the moment assumptions.
source_ids: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

slides.title: 1.5 Regression and Sampling Designs
slides.subtitle: Designed vs. observational data
bullets: Terminology: dependent/independent, response/treatment, regressand/regressor
Designed studies: RAND Health Insurance Experiment (14 plans, 6 cities)
Observational data: Galton heights, confounding variables (e.g., diet)
Statistical control replaces experimental control
slides.speaker_notes: Stress that actuarial data is almost always observational, so causal claims require careful statistical control rather than randomization.
source_ids: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

slides.title: 1.6 Actuarial Applications of Regression
slides.subtitle: Pricing, reserving, solvency testing
bullets: Pricing: risk classification counters adverse selection
Reserving: forecasting future obligations
Solvency testing: assessing capital adequacy
Regression as a shared quantitative toolkit across all three
slides.speaker_notes: Connect each of the three traditional actuarial areas back to regression, using the adverse-selection mechanism as the concrete pricing example.
source_ids: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

slides.title: 1.8 Exercises Overview
slides.subtitle: Seven applied datasets
bullets: MEPS Health Expenditures (n=2,000)
Wisconsin Nursing Home Utilization (362/355 facilities)
AutoClaims (n=6,773), Hospital Costs (n=500)
AutoBI (n=1,340), NAICExpense (n=500), UN Life Expectancy (n=185)
slides.speaker_notes: Preview the practice datasets students will use to apply histograms, qq plots, and log transforms to real actuarial and health data.
source_ids: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

slides.title: 1.9 Technical Supplement — Central Limit Theorem
slides.subtitle: Why normal approximations work
bullets: CLT: sqrt(n)/sigma * (ybar-mu) -> standard normal as n grows
Adequate for n=25 to 50 in most practical cases
Edgeworth Approximation adds a skewness-correction term
Regression coefficients are weighted averages, inheriting CLT normality
slides.speaker_notes: Tie the whole chapter together: transformations toward symmetry (Section 1.3) make the CLT/Edgeworth approximations more accurate for regression inference.
source_ids: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

slides.title: What to Carry Away
slides.subtitle: Discussion
bullets: Regression quantifies relationships while controlling for explanatory variables
The normal curve and its transforms underpin classical inference
Observational actuarial data demands statistical, not experimental, control
Pricing, reserving, and solvency testing all rely on these foundations
slides.speaker_notes: Close by asking learners to identify which of their own datasets are observational vs designed, and where a log transform might help.
source_ids: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex
